claim: The human brain contains approximately 86 billion neurons.
source: The human brain contains approximately 86 billion neurons, and each neuron engages in several thousand specific synaptic connections, resulting in complex neural networks with over 1015 specific connections.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in neuroscience, representing established scientific knowledge.

claim: Each neuron engages in several thousand specific synaptic connections.
source: The human brain contains approximately 86 billion neurons, and each neuron engages in several thousand specific synaptic connections, resulting in complex neural networks with over 1015 specific connections.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about neuronal connectivity.

claim: Complex neural circuits are required for normal brain function.
source: These complex neural circuits are required for normal brain function, and inappropriate assemblies of neural circuits underlie neurodevelopmental and neuropsychiatric disorders (Hyman, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hyman, 2008.

claim: Inappropriate assemblies of neural circuits underlie neurodevelopmental and neuropsychiatric disorders.
source: These complex neural circuits are required for normal brain function, and inappropriate assemblies of neural circuits underlie neurodevelopmental and neuropsychiatric disorders (Hyman, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hyman, 2008.

claim: Long-distance neuronal migration from the site of origin to the final destination is a remarkable feature of neurodevelopment.
source: A remarkable feature of neurodevelopment is the long-distance neuronal migration from the site of origin to the final destination (Angevine and Sidman, 1961; Ayala et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Angevine and Sidman, 1961 and Ayala et al., 2007.

claim: Cortical immature neurons generated from the proliferative ventricular and subventricular zones migrate radially through specific phases to appropriate laminar positions in an 'inside-out' manner.
source: For example, cortical immature neurons generated from the proliferative ventricular and subventricular zones (VZ/SVZ) migrate radially through specific phases to appropriate laminar positions in an 'inside-out' manner and then differentiate into distinct subtypes of cortical neurons (Angevine and Sidman, 1961; LoTurco and Bai, 2006; Rakic, 1974).
evidence: Supported by citations to Angevine and Sidman, 1961; LoTurco and Bai, 2006; Rakic, 1974.

claim: Cortical migration phases include somal translocation, multipolar migration, and glial-guided locomotion.
source: The cortical migration phases include somal translocation, multipolar migration, and glial-guided locomotion (Ayala et al., 2007; Cooper, 2014; Noctor et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ayala et al., 2007; Cooper, 2014; Noctor et al., 2004.

claim: Newly born bipolar neurons in SVZ assume multipolar or stellate morphology and migrate randomly in the intermediate zone.
source: Newly born bipolar neurons in SVZ assume multipolar or stellate morphology and migrate randomly in the intermediate zone (IZ), moving tangentially, up, or down (Ayala et al., 2007; Cooper, 2014; Jossin and Cooper, 2011; Nadarajah et al., 2003; Noctor et al., 2004; Tabata and Nakajima, 2003).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations.

claim: Multipolar neurons transit into bipolar again near the border of IZ/CP and resume final radial migration to settle in appropriate cortical layers.
source: They then transit into bipolar again near the border of IZ/CP (cortical plate) and resume final radial migration to settle in appropriate cortical layers (Ayala et al., 2007; Cooper, 2014; Jossin and Cooper, 2011; Nadarajah et al., 2003; Noctor et al., 2004; Tabata and Nakajima, 2003).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations.

claim: Abnormal neuronal migration results in various neurodevelopmental and psychiatric diseases.
source: Abnormal neuronal migration results in various neurodevelopmental and psychiatric diseases (Ayala et al., 2007; LoTurco and Bai, 2006; Valiente and Marín, 2010); however, the underlying molecular mechanisms for the abnormal neuronal migration is largely unknown.
evidence: Supported by citations to Ayala et al., 2007; LoTurco and Bai, 2006; Valiente and Marín, 2010.

claim: The underlying molecular mechanisms for abnormal neuronal migration are largely unknown.
source: Abnormal neuronal migration results in various neurodevelopmental and psychiatric diseases (Ayala et al., 2007; LoTurco and Bai, 2006; Valiente and Marín, 2010); however, the underlying molecular mechanisms for the abnormal neuronal migration is largely unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Human genetics studies have implicated mutations of the clustered protocadherin cell adhesion genes in the 5q31 region for various developmental and psychiatric disorders.
source: Human genetics studies have implicated mutations of the clustered protocadherin (Pcdh) cell adhesion genes in the 5q31 region for various developmental and psychiatric disorders (Anitha et al., 2013; Iossifov et al., 2012; Pedrosa et al., 2008; Shimojima et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Anitha et al., 2013; Iossifov et al., 2012; Pedrosa et al., 2008; Shimojima et al., 2011.

claim: Diverse clustered Pcdh genes play an important role in establishing neuronal identity and connectivity in the vertebrate brain.
source: Similar to Dscam1 in Drosophila (Zipursky and Sanes, 2010), diverse clustered Pcdh genes play an important role in establishing neuronal identity and connectivity in the vertebrate brain (Garrett et al., 2012; Lefebvre et al., 2012; Molumby et al., 2016; Nicoludis et al., 2016; Rubinstein et al., 2015; Schreiner and Weiner, 2010; Suo et al., 2012; Thu et al., 2014; Wu and Maniatis, 1999).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations.

claim: In mice, 58 clustered Pcdh genes are organized into three closely linked Pcdh α, β, and γ clusters.
source: In mice, 58 clustered Pcdh genes are organized into three closely linked Pcdh α, β, and γ clusters (Pcdha, Pcdhb, and Pcdhg) (Wu et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wu et al., 2001.

claim: The Pcdh α and γ clusters are each consisted of variable and constant regions, similar to that of the Ig, Tcr, and Ugt1 gene clusters.
source: The Pcdh α and γ clusters are each consisted of variable and constant regions, similar to that of the Ig, Tcr, and Ugt1 gene clusters (Wu, 2005; Wu and Maniatis, 1999; Wu et al., 2001; Zhang et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wu, 2005; Wu and Maniatis, 1999; Wu et al., 2001; Zhang et al., 2004.

claim: The variable region of the mouse Pcdhα cluster contains 12 highly similar 'alternate exons', α1-α12, whose promoters are stochastically activated by distal enhancers.
source: In particular, the variable region of the mouse Pcdhα cluster contains 12 highly similar 'alternate exons', α1-α12, whose promoters are stochastically activated by distal enhancers, and two divergent c-type 'ubiquitous exons', αc1 and αc2, whose promoters are constitutively activated by distal enhancers (Figure 1A) (Guo et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Guo et al., 2012 and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: The variable region of the mouse Pcdhα cluster contains two divergent c-type 'ubiquitous exons', αc1 and αc2, whose promoters are constitutively activated by distal enhancers.
source: In particular, the variable region of the mouse Pcdhα cluster contains 12 highly similar 'alternate exons', α1-α12, whose promoters are stochastically activated by distal enhancers, and two divergent c-type 'ubiquitous exons', αc1 and αc2, whose promoters are constitutively activated by distal enhancers (Figure 1A) (Guo et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Guo et al., 2012 and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Each variable exon is separately spliced to the common set of downstream constant exons, generating diverse mRNAs and proteins.
source: Each variable exon is separately spliced to the common set of downstream constant exons, generating diverse mRNAs and proteins.
evidence: This is a statement about the molecular mechanism of Pcdhα gene expression.

claim: CCCTC-binding factor (CTCF)/Cohesin-mediated topological chromatin-looping domains are crucial for proper expression of Pcdhα proteins.
source: CCCTC-binding factor (CTCF)/Cohesin-mediated topological chromatin-looping domains are crucial for proper expression of Pcdhα proteins (Guo et al., 2015; Huang and Wu, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Guo et al., 2015; Huang and Wu, 2016.

claim: Each variable exon encodes an extracellular domain (ectodomain EC1-6), a transmembrane segment, and a juxtamembrane variable cytoplasmic domain (VCD).
source: Each variable exon encodes an extracellular domain (ectodomain EC1-6), a transmembrane segment, and a juxtamembrane variable cytoplasmic domain (VCD) (Shonubi et al., 2015; Wu and Maniatis, 1999), whereas the three constant exons encode a common membrane-distal constant domain (CD) of all Pcdhα proteins (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by citations to Shonubi et al., 2015; Wu and Maniatis, 1999 and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: The three constant exons encode a common membrane-distal constant domain (CD) of all Pcdhα proteins.
source: Each variable exon encodes an extracellular domain (ectodomain EC1-6), a transmembrane segment, and a juxtamembrane variable cytoplasmic domain (VCD) (Shonubi et al., 2015; Wu and Maniatis, 1999), whereas the three constant exons encode a common membrane-distal constant domain (CD) of all Pcdhα proteins (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by citations to Shonubi et al., 2015; Wu and Maniatis, 1999 and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Diverse extracellular cues converge on a single intracellular signaling pathway in Pcdhα proteins.
source: This suggests that diverse extracellular cues converge on a single intracellular signaling pathway.
evidence: This is inferred from the structure of Pcdhα proteins with diverse extracellular domains but a common intracellular constant domain.

claim: The functional significance of the Pcdhα genomic arrangement remains obscure.
source: However, the functional significance of this intriguing arrangement remains obscure.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: A large family of cell-surface receptors, including Pcdhα6, recruit WAVE complex to the plasma membrane.
source: A large family of cell-surface receptors, including Pcdhα6 (Pcdha6), recruit WAVE complex to the plasma membrane (Chen et al., 2014; Nakao et al., 2008; Tai et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chen et al., 2014; Nakao et al., 2008; Tai et al., 2010.

claim: The WAVE complex is a conserved two-partite pentameric complex consisting of a pseudosymmetric dimer of Sra1/Cyfip1 and Nap1/Hem2, and a heteromeric trimer of HSPC300/Brick, Abi1/2/3, and WAVE1/2/3/SCAR.
source: The WAVE complex is a conserved two-partite pentameric complex consisting of a pseudosymmetric dimer of Sra1/Cyfip1 and Nap1/Hem2, and a heteromeric trimer of HSPC300/Brick, Abi1/2/3, and WAVE1/2/3/SCAR (Chen et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chen et al., 2010.

claim: Abi2 interacts with Abelson tyrosine kinase (Abl kinase) and has been implicated in cortical radial migration.
source: First, Abi2 interacts with Abelson tyrosine kinase (Abl kinase) and has been implicated in cortical radial migration (Xie et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Xie et al., 2013.

claim: WAVEs/SCARs are members of the Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome protein (WASP) and WASP verprolin homologous protein family, defined by a conserved VCA domain.
source: Second, WAVEs/SCARs are members of the Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome protein (WASP) and WASP verprolin homologous protein family, defined by a conserved VCA domain (verprolin homologous, cofilin homologous or central hydrophobic, and acidic regions) (Chen et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chen et al., 2010.

claim: VCA is inhibited by intermolecular interaction with Sra1 and intramolecular interaction within WAVE.
source: Third, VCA is inhibited by intermolecular interaction with Sra1 and intramolecular interaction within WAVE (Chen et al., 2010; Padrick et al., 2011; Rohatgi et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chen et al., 2010; Padrick et al., 2011; Rohatgi et al., 1999.

claim: Rac1 binds to WAVE complex and induces a conformational change to release VCA from its inhibitory state and to activate actin filament nucleation and branching through the Arp2/3 complex.
source: Fourth, Rac1 binds to WAVE complex and induces a conformational change to release VCA from its inhibitory state and to activate actin filament nucleation and branching through the Arp2/3 complex (Chen et al., 2010; Lebensohn and Kirschner, 2009; Padrick et al., 2011; Rohatgi et al., 1999; Ti et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chen et al., 2010; Lebensohn and Kirschner, 2009; Padrick et al., 2011; Rohatgi et al., 1999; Ti et al., 2011.

claim: Whether and how WAVE complex and Pyk2 kinase function in cortical neuron migration are not clear.
source: However, whether and how WAVE complex and Pyk2 kinase function in cortical neuron migration are not clear.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Pcdhα proteins play a critical role in neuronal migration and cytoskeletal dynamics.
source: Here, we report that Pcdhα proteins play a critical role in neuronal migration and cytoskeletal dynamics.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Pcdhα regulates lamellipodial and filopodial dynamics and neuronal migration as well as dendrite morphogenesis through interaction with WAVE complex via the WIRS motif of Pcdhα constant domain.
source: Specifically, we define an actin cytoskeleton remodeling pathway by which Pcdhα regulates lamellipodial and filopodial dynamics and neuronal migration as well as dendrite morphogenesis through interaction with WAVE complex via the WIRS (WAVE interacting receptor sequence) motif of Pcdhα constant domain (CD).
evidence: This is a main finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Pyk2 regulates cortical neuron migration by inactivating the small GTPase Rac1.
source: In addition, Pyk2 regulates cortical neuron migration by inactivating the small GTPase Rac1.
evidence: This is a main finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Pcdhα proteins are expressed throughout the developing forebrain.
source: We mapped the embryonic expression pattern of Pcdhα by using a GFP knockin mouse line (PcdhαGFP) (Wu et al., 2007) and found that Pcdhα proteins are expressed throughout the developing forebrain (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B using a GFP knockin mouse line.

claim: Pcdhα proteins are expressed in all cortical regions and most prominently in the intermediate zone and marginal zone of the developing neocortex.
source: Immunostaining with an antibody against alpha constant domain (αCD) revealed that Pcdhα proteins are expressed in all cortical regions and most prominently in the intermediate zone and marginal zone (IZ and MZ) of the developing neocortex (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Starting at E10, every member of the Pcdhα cluster is expressed in the developing brain.
source: RT-PCR with isoform-specific primers showed that, starting at E10, every member of the Pcdhα cluster is expressed in the developing brain (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Pcdhα knockdown with two independent shRNAs results in a significant decrease of migrating neurons in the cortical plate and a concomitant increase within the lower intermediate zone.
source: Pcdhα knockdown (αKD) with two independent shRNAs, each targeting a distinct subdomain of the constant region by in utero electroporation (IUE), revealed a significant decrease of migrating neurons in the cortical plate (CP) and a concomitant increase within the lower intermediate zone, suggesting defects in multipolar migration (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Pcdhα knockdown results in defects in multipolar migration.
source: Pcdhα knockdown (αKD) with two independent shRNAs, each targeting a distinct subdomain of the constant region by in utero electroporation (IUE), revealed a significant decrease of migrating neurons in the cortical plate (CP) and a concomitant increase within the lower intermediate zone, suggesting defects in multipolar migration (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing altered distribution of neurons.

claim: The αKD multipolar neurons in the intermediate zone display stunted processes.
source: The αKD multipolar neurons in the intermediate zone display stunted processes, as shown by lucida drawings (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by lucida drawings shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Live cell imaging of brain organotypic slice culture demonstrated the slower velocity of multipolar migration of αKD neurons compared to controls.
source: Live cell imaging of brain organotypic slice culture demonstrated the slower velocity of multipolar migration of αKD neurons compared to controls (Figure 1F–H and Video 1).
evidence: Supported by live cell imaging data shown in Figure 1F–H and Video 1.

claim: Early born αKD neurons also have migration defects.
source: In addition, early born αKD neurons also have migration defects, suggesting that Pcdhα is also required for glia-independent somal translocation (Figure 1I and J).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1I and J.

claim: Pcdhα is required for glia-independent somal translocation.
source: In addition, early born αKD neurons also have migration defects, suggesting that Pcdhα is also required for glia-independent somal translocation (Figure 1I and J).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that early born neurons also have migration defects.

claim: Pcdhα is required for migration of immature cortical neurons.
source: This suggests that Pcdhα is required for migration of immature cortical neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing migration defects in αKD neurons.

claim: αKD results in no significant difference of percentage of BrdU+ cells compared with controls.
source: Compared with controls, αKD results in no significant difference of percentage of BrdU+ cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: Supported by BrdU labeling data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: αKD does not alter the percentage of Tbr2+ intermediate progenitor cells.
source: In addition, αKD does not alter the percentage of Tbr2+intermediate progenitor cells (IPCs) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E and F), nor the morphology of brain lipid binding protein (BLBP)-labeled radial glia cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E and F.

claim: αKD does not alter the morphology of brain lipid binding protein (BLBP)-labeled radial glia cells.
source: In addition, αKD does not alter the percentage of Tbr2+intermediate progenitor cells (IPCs) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E and F), nor the morphology of brain lipid binding protein (BLBP)-labeled radial glia cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G.

claim: The migration defect is not due to increased apoptosis.
source: Moreover, the defect is not due to increased apoptosis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: Supported by apoptosis assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1H.

claim: There is no cortical migration defect in mice with deletion of the entire Pcdhα cluster.
source: Finally, there is no cortical migration defect (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I) in mice with deletion of the entire Pcdhα cluster (αKO) (Wu et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1I.

claim: The phenotypic discrepancy between αKD and αKO may be due to known genetic compensation mechanisms induced by deletion but not knockdown.
source: The phenotypic discrepancy may be due to known genetic compensation mechanisms induced by deletion but not knockdown (Rossi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculation based on known genetic compensation mechanisms, supported by citation to Rossi et al., 2015.

claim: The single α6* isoform rescues the αKD migration defect.
source: Indeed the single α6* isoform rescues the αKD migration defect.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data, though the specific figure is not mentioned in this sentence.

claim: Pcdh αc1* rescues the migration defect.
source: The Pcdh αc1* also rescues the migration defect; however, αc2* does not (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: αc2* does not rescue the migration defect.
source: The Pcdh αc1* also rescues the migration defect; however, αc2* does not (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: αc2 has distinct functions other than cortical neuron migration.
source: This suggests that αc2 has distinct functions other than cortical neuron migration, consistent with very recent findings that αc2 endows serotonergic neurons with a single cell-type identity and specifically mediates the axonal tiling and assembly of serotonergic neural circuitries (Chen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data and supported by citation to Chen et al., 2017.

claim: Myr-α6ICD* and Myr-αc1ICD* rescue the migration defect.
source: We found that Myr-α6ICD* and Myr-αc1ICD* rescue the migration defect, and Myr-αc2ICD* does not (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: Myr-αc2ICD* does not rescue the migration defect.
source: We found that Myr-α6ICD* and Myr-αc1ICD* rescue the migration defect, and Myr-αc2ICD* does not (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: The intracellular domain of Pcdhα plays an important role in cortical neuron migration.
source: This suggests that the intracellular domain of Pcdhα plays an important role in cortical neuron migration.
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue experiments with myristoylated intracellular domains.

claim: Myr-αCD* rescues the migration defect.
source: Intriguingly, we found that Myr-αCD* rescues the migration defect (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: αc2 variable cytoplasmic domain has an inhibitory function.
source: This demonstrated that αc2 variable cytoplasmic domain has an inhibitory function.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Myr-αCD* rescues the migration defect while Myr-αc2ICD* does not.

claim: αc2 variable cytoplasmic domain is the longest and most divergent among those of αc1 as well as of α1-α12.
source: Consistently, sequence analysis revealed that αc2 variable cytoplasmic domain is the longest and most divergent among those of αc1 as well as of α1-α12 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Members of the Pcdhα family except αc2 regulate cortical neuron migration through their common constant domain.
source: Together, these data suggest that members of the Pcdhα family except αc2 regulate cortical neuron migration through their common constant domain.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the rescue experiments with various Pcdhα constructs.

claim: Overexpression of either WAVE2 or Abi2 in vivo rescues the cortical neuron migration defect of αKD neurons.
source: Remarkably, we found that overexpression of either WAVE2 (Wasf2) or Abi2 in vivo rescues the cortical neuron migration defect of αKD neurons (Figure 2B) although they themselves have no apparent influence on cortical neuron migration (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and 2C.

claim: WAVE2 and Abi2 themselves have no apparent influence on cortical neuron migration.
source: Remarkably, we found that overexpression of either WAVE2 (Wasf2) or Abi2 in vivo rescues the cortical neuron migration defect of αKD neurons (Figure 2B) although they themselves have no apparent influence on cortical neuron migration (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Endogenous Pcdhα and WAVE2 co-localize in primary cultured cortical neurons.
source: Consistently, endogenous Pcdhα and WAVE2 co-localize in primary cultured cortical neurons (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2D and E.

claim: Mutating the WIRS motif of α6*, αc1*, and Myr-αCD* abolishes the rescue effect.
source: In addition, mutating the WIRS motif (from FITFGK to FIAAGK) of α6*, αc1*, and Myr-αCD* (α6*-AA, αc1*-AA, and Myr-αCD*-AA) abolishes the rescue effect (Figure 2F and G, in comparison to Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F and G.

claim: WIRS-mutated isoforms as well as wild types appear to reach the plasma membrane.
source: As controls, these WIRS-mutated isoforms as well as wild types appears to reach the plasma membrane (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Pcdhα regulates cortical neuron migration through the WAVE complex.
source: Thus, Pcdhα regulates cortical neuron migration through the WAVE complex.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the rescue experiments with WAVE2 and Abi2, and the WIRS motif mutations.

claim: Pcdhα physically interacts with and negatively regulates the Pyk2 kinase.
source: Pcdhα physically interacts with and negatively regulates the Pyk2 kinase (Chen et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chen et al., 2009.

claim: Pcdhα regulates dendritic and spine morphogenesis through inhibiting Pyk2 activity.
source: In addition, we previously found that Pcdhα regulates dendritic and spine morphogenesis through inhibiting Pyk2 activity (Suo et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Suo et al., 2012.

claim: Pyk2 knockdown per se does not affect cortical neuron migration.
source: Although Pyk2 (Ptk2b) knockdown (Pyk2KD) per se or CRISPR knockout of Pyk2 (Pyk2KO) does not affect cortical neuron migration (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), we found that Pyk2KD rescues the defect of cortical neuron migration in αKD (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: CRISPR knockout of Pyk2 does not affect cortical neuron migration.
source: Although Pyk2 (Ptk2b) knockdown (Pyk2KD) per se or CRISPR knockout of Pyk2 (Pyk2KO) does not affect cortical neuron migration (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), we found that Pyk2KD rescues the defect of cortical neuron migration in αKD (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Pyk2KD rescues the defect of cortical neuron migration in αKD.
source: Although Pyk2 (Ptk2b) knockdown (Pyk2KD) per se or CRISPR knockout of Pyk2 (Pyk2KO) does not affect cortical neuron migration (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), we found that Pyk2KD rescues the defect of cortical neuron migration in αKD (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Pcdhα regulates cortical neuron migration, at least in part, through the inhibition of Pyk2.
source: This suggests that Pcdhα regulates cortical neuron migration, at least in part, through the inhibition of Pyk2.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Pyk2KD rescues the migration defect in αKD.

claim: The majority of Pyk2OE cells are stalled in the middle intermediate zone.
source: We found that the majority of Pyk2OE cells are stalled in the middle intermediate zone (mIZ) (Figure 3B), a stage little later than the stalling of αKD cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: mIZ Pyk2OE cells have aberrant multipolar morphology with supernumerary primary processes in comparison to single leading processes of control cells.
source: In addition, these mIZ cells have aberrant multipolar morphology with supernumerary primary processes in comparison to single leading processes of control cells (Figure 3C–E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C–E.

claim: The very few Pyk2OE cells in the lower cortical plate harbor elaborated leading processes.
source: For the very few Pyk2OE cells in the lower cortical plate (CP), they harbor elaborated leading processes (Figure 3F and G); by contrast, control cells displayed typical bipolar morphology with a single or bifurcated thick leading process (Figure 3F and G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F and G.

claim: Control cells displayed typical bipolar morphology with a single or bifurcated thick leading process.
source: For the very few Pyk2OE cells in the lower cortical plate (CP), they harbor elaborated leading processes (Figure 3F and G); by contrast, control cells displayed typical bipolar morphology with a single or bifurcated thick leading process (Figure 3F and G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F and G.

claim: Pyk2OE leads to the inhibition of Rac1 activity.
source: Pyk2OE leads to the inhibition of Rac1 activity (Suo et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Suo et al., 2012.

claim: Loss of Rac1 activity leads to aberrant actin polymerization at many sites with no controlled spatial information, resulting in supernumerary primary processes.
source: As Rac1 is thought to provide the spatial information for actin polymerization (Tahirovic et al., 2010), loss of Rac1 activity leads to aberrant actin polymerization at many sites with no controlled spatial information, resulting in supernumerary primary processes (Figure 3C–E) and more branchy morphology (Figure 3F and G).
evidence: This is inferred from the known role of Rac1 in actin polymerization, supported by citation to Tahirovic et al., 2010.

claim: There is a significant difference of velocity of cortical neuron migration between Pyk2OE and control cells.
source: Finally, time-lapse imaging showed that there is a significant difference of velocity of cortical neuron migration between Pyk2OE and control cells (Figure 3H and I, and Video 2).
evidence: Supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 3H and I, and Video 2.

claim: Pyk2OE partially recapitulates cortical neuron migration defects.
source: These data suggest that Pyk2OE partially recapitulates cortical neuron migration defects.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing migration defects in Pyk2OE neurons.

claim: Most Golgi complexes are normally localized in front of the cell nucleus and are oriented toward the cortical plate.
source: Most Golgi complexes are normally localized in front of the cell nucleus and are oriented toward the cortical plate (Jossin and Cooper, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jossin and Cooper, 2011.

claim: The polarity of most Pyk2OE cells is disrupted, showing oblique or inverted orientation of the Golgi apparatus.
source: However, the polarity of most Pyk2OE cells is disrupted, showing oblique or inverted orientation of the Golgi apparatus (Figure 3J and K).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3J and K.

claim: Pyk2OE blocks multipolar-bipolar transition by disrupting proper localization of the Golgi apparatus.
source: Thus, Pyk2OE blocks multipolar-bipolar transition by disrupting proper localization of the Golgi apparatus.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing disrupted Golgi orientation in Pyk2OE cells.

claim: Early-born Pyk2OE neurons are also stalled at the intermediate zone.
source: Finally, early-born Pyk2OE neurons are also stalled at the intermediate zone, suggesting that Pyk2 also plays a role in somal translocation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: Pyk2 plays a role in somal translocation.
source: Finally, early-born Pyk2OE neurons are also stalled at the intermediate zone, suggesting that Pyk2 also plays a role in somal translocation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that early-born Pyk2OE neurons are stalled at the intermediate zone.

claim: Pyk2OE under the NeuroD promoter significantly impairs cortical neuron migration in postmitotic neurons.
source: We found that Pyk2OE under the NeuroD promoter also significantly impairs cortical neuron migration in postmitotic neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E-G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E-G.

claim: Pcdhα regulates cortical neuron migration, at least in part, through inhibiting Pyk2 kinase activity.
source: Taken together, this suggests that Pcdhα regulates cortical neuron migration, at least in part, through inhibiting Pyk2 kinase activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing that Pyk2KD rescues αKD migration defects and Pyk2OE impairs migration.

claim: Rac1 is epistatic downstream of Pyk2 in dendrite development and spine morphogenesis.
source: We previously found that Rac1 is epistatic downstream of Pyk2 in dendrite development and spine morphogenesis (Suo et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Suo et al., 2012.

claim: Rac1Q61L rescues defects of multipolar migration and morphology of Pyk2OE neurons.
source: We found that Rac1Q61L rescues defects of multipolar migration and morphology of Pyk2OE neurons (Figure 4A–C), although Rac1Q61L itself has no apparent effect on cortical neuron migration (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A–C.

claim: Rac1Q61L itself has no apparent effect on cortical neuron migration.
source: We found that Rac1Q61L rescues defects of multipolar migration and morphology of Pyk2OE neurons (Figure 4A–C), although Rac1Q61L itself has no apparent effect on cortical neuron migration (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Overexpression of Rac1G12V impairs cortical neuron migration.
source: However, overexpression of another constitutively active form of Rac1 (Rac1G12V) impairs cortical neuron migration (Figure 4D) (Konno et al., 2005) and cannot be used to rescue, likely because it has a lower affinity for GTP and thus lower constitutive activity than Rac1Q61L.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D and citation to Konno et al., 2005.

claim: Rac1G12V has a lower affinity for GTP and thus lower constitutive activity than Rac1Q61L.
source: However, overexpression of another constitutively active form of Rac1 (Rac1G12V) impairs cortical neuron migration (Figure 4D) (Konno et al., 2005) and cannot be used to rescue, likely because it has a lower affinity for GTP and thus lower constitutive activity than Rac1Q61L.
evidence: This is a speculation about the biochemical properties of Rac1G12V.

claim: The two constitutively active forms of Rac1 have distinct roles in cortical neuron migration.
source: Thus, the two constitutively active forms of Rac1 have distinct roles in cortical neuron migration (Figure 4A and D).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing different effects of Rac1Q61L and Rac1G12V.

claim: Pyk2OE inhibits multipolar-bipolar transition and leads to aberrant branchy morphology in the intermediate zone by inactivating the small GTPase Rac1.
source: Together, we conclude that Pyk2OE inhibits multipolar-bipolar transition and leads to aberrant branchy morphology in the intermediate zone by inactivating the small GTPase Rac1.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing that Rac1Q61L rescues Pyk2OE defects.

claim: Pyk2 functions as an enzyme through its middle kinase domain and as a molecular scaffold through its N-terminal FERM domain.
source: Pyk2 functions as an enzyme through its middle kinase domain and as a molecular scaffold through its N-terminal FERM (four-point-one, ezrin, radixin, moesin) domain (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) (Chen et al., 2009; Lev et al., 1995; Suo et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chen et al., 2009; Lev et al., 1995; Suo et al., 2012 and reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Overexpression of Pyk2Y402F, Pyk2Y579F, Pyk2Y580F, and Pyk2Y881F still recapitulate the migration defects of αKD.
source: We found that overexpression of Pyk2Y402F, an autophosphorylation mutant that still can be activated by endogenous Pyk2, as well as Pyk2Y579F, Pyk2Y580F, and Pyk2Y881F, still recapitulate the migration defects of αKD (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Overexpression of Pyk2K457A cannot recapitulate the migration defects of αKD.
source: However, overexpression of Pyk2K457A, which has a mutation at the catalytic center and is completely kinase-dead (Suo et al., 2012), cannot recapitulate the migration defects of αKD (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: The catalytic activity of overexpressed Pyk2 is essential for recapitulating the migration defects of αKD.
source: This suggests that the catalytic activity of overexpressed Pyk2 is essential for recapitulating the migration defects of αKD.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that kinase-dead Pyk2K457A cannot recapitulate the migration defects.

claim: Overexpression of the Pyk2 FERM domain alone recapitulates the blocking activity of Pyk2OE.
source: Remarkably, overexpression of the Pyk2 FERM domain alone recapitulates the blocking activity of Pyk2OE (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and C), whereas deletion of FERM domain abolishes the blocking (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and C.

claim: Deletion of FERM domain abolishes the blocking activity of Pyk2OE.
source: Remarkably, overexpression of the Pyk2 FERM domain alone recapitulates the blocking activity of Pyk2OE (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and C), whereas deletion of FERM domain abolishes the blocking (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and C.

claim: The C-terminal FAT domain of Pyk2 is not required for the blocking effect.
source: Consistently, the C-terminal FAT domain of Pyk2 is not required for the blocking effect and the kinase domain alone cannot block cortical neuron migration (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and C.

claim: The kinase domain alone cannot block cortical neuron migration.
source: Consistently, the C-terminal FAT domain of Pyk2 is not required for the blocking effect and the kinase domain alone cannot block cortical neuron migration (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and C.

claim: Pyk2 has important kinase-independent functions in contextual fear memory.
source: This is consistent with that Pyk2 has important kinase-independent functions in contextual fear memory (Suo et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Suo et al., 2017.

claim: Both Pyk2 kinase cascade and FERM scaffold are crucial for blocking cortical neuron migration.
source: Together, we conclude that both Pyk2 kinase cascade and FERM scaffold are crucial for blocking cortical neuron migration.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data with various Pyk2 mutants.

claim: Rac1Q61L cannot rescue the blocking activity of FERM domain.
source: However, we found that Rac1Q61L cannot rescue the blocking activity of FERM domain (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Constitutive active form of Rac1 only functions downstream of the kinase cascade but not the FERM scaffold of Pyk2.
source: This suggests that constitutive active form of Rac1 only functions downstream of the kinase cascade but not the FERM scaffold of Pyk2.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Rac1Q61L cannot rescue the FERM domain blocking activity.

claim: The size of lamellipodia around cell cortex in αKD neurons decreases significantly compared with controls at stage 1.
source: At stage 1, we found that the size of lamellipodia around cell cortex in αKD neurons decreases significantly compared with controls (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: α6*, αc1*, or Myr-αCD* rescues the αKD lamellipodial defect at stage 1.
source: In addition, α6*, αc1*, or Myr-αCD* rescues the αKD lamellipodial defect.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data, though the specific figure is not mentioned in this sentence.

claim: αc2* does not rescue the αKD lamellipodial defect at stage 1.
source: By contrast, αc2* does not rescue (Figure 5C and D), which is consistent with that αc2* cannot rescue the defects of cortical neuron migration (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C and D.

claim: Mutating the WIRS motif in either α6*, αc1*, or Myr-αCD* abolishes their rescue effects on lamellipodial defects at stage 1.
source: Moreover, mutating the WIRS motif (from FITFGK to FIAAGK) in either α6*, αc1*, or Myr-αCD* abolishes their rescue effects (Figure 5E and F), similar to the situation in cortical neuron migration (Figure 2G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E and F.

claim: Both WAVE2 and Abi2 rescue the lamellipodial defect at stage 1.
source: Finally, both WAVE2 and Abi2 rescue the lamellipodial defect (Figure 5G and H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G and H.

claim: αKD results in a significant decrease of percentage of primary neurites with lamellipodia-like protrusions at stage 2.
source: At stage 2, αKD results in a significant decrease of percentage of primary neurites with lamellipodia-like protrusions (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: α6*, αc1*, or Myr-αCD* rescues the αKD lamellipodial defect at stage 2 while αc2* does not.
source: Consistent with the situation at stage 1, α6*, αc1*, or Myr-αCD* rescues this αKD lamellipodial defect while αc2* does not (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and D), and mutating the WIRS motif (from FITFGK to FIAAGK) abolishes the rescue effects of either α6*, αc1*, or Myr-αCD* (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E and F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: Mutating the WIRS motif abolishes the rescue effects of either α6*, αc1*, or Myr-αCD* on lamellipodial defects at stage 2.
source: Consistent with the situation at stage 1, α6*, αc1*, or Myr-αCD* rescues this αKD lamellipodial defect while αc2* does not (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and D), and mutating the WIRS motif (from FITFGK to FIAAGK) abolishes the rescue effects of either α6*, αc1*, or Myr-αCD* (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E and F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E and F.

claim: Both WAVE2 and Abi2 rescue the lamellipodial defect of stage 2 αKD neurons.
source: In addition, consistent with stage 1, both WAVE2 and Abi2 rescue the lamellipodial defect of stage 2 αKD neurons (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G and H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1G and H.

claim: αKD lamellipodial dynamics are significantly impaired in comparison with control neurons.
source: Finally, αKD lamellipodial dynamics are significantly impaired in comparison with control neurons, whose veil-like lamellipodia are motile and are constantly extending and retracting in both stage 1 and stage 2 neurons (Figure 5I, Figure 5—figure supplement 1I, Video 3 and Video 4).
evidence: Supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 5I, Figure 5—figure supplement 1I, Video 3 and Video 4.

claim: Pcdhα is indispensable for lamellipodial dynamics.
source: These data demonstrated that Pcdhα is indispensable for lamellipodial dynamics.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing impaired lamellipodial dynamics in αKD neurons.

claim: Lamellipodial dynamics are essential for cell migration.
source: Because lamellipodial dynamics are essential for cell migration (Krause and Gautreau, 2014), this suggests that cortical neuron migration defects of αKD are a consequence of impairment of lamellipodial formation and cytoskeletal dynamics.
evidence: Supported by citation to Krause and Gautreau, 2014.

claim: Cortical neuron migration defects of αKD are a consequence of impairment of lamellipodial formation and cytoskeletal dynamics.
source: Because lamellipodial dynamics are essential for cell migration (Krause and Gautreau, 2014), this suggests that cortical neuron migration defects of αKD are a consequence of impairment of lamellipodial formation and cytoskeletal dynamics.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that αKD impairs lamellipodial dynamics and migration.

claim: Knockdown of Pyk2 in αKD cells results in a significant increase of lamellipodial sizes of stage1 neurons.
source: Consistent with that Pyk2KD rescues cortical neuron migration defects of PcdhαKD (Figure 3A), we found that knockdown of Pyk2 in αKD cells results in a significant increase of lamellipodial sizes of stage1 neurons as well as of the percentage of primary neurites with lamellipodia of stage2 neurons (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A–C.

claim: Knockdown of Pyk2 in αKD cells results in a significant increase of the percentage of primary neurites with lamellipodia of stage2 neurons.
source: Consistent with that Pyk2KD rescues cortical neuron migration defects of PcdhαKD (Figure 3A), we found that knockdown of Pyk2 in αKD cells results in a significant increase of lamellipodial sizes of stage1 neurons as well as of the percentage of primary neurites with lamellipodia of stage2 neurons (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A–C.

claim: Pyk2OE results in a significant decrease of lamellipodial sizes.
source: In addition, Pyk2OE results in a significant decrease of lamellipodial sizes, consistent with that of αKD (Figure 6D and E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D and E.

claim: Pyk2OE results in a significant increase of filopodial number per stage 1 neuron.
source: Filopodia are thin membrane protrusion pushed by underlying actin bundles and filopodial formation is also dependent on Arp2/3 complex (Mattila and Lappalainen, 2008), we found that Pyk2OE results in a significant increase of filopodial number per stage 1 neuron as well as of primary neurite number per stage 2 neuron despite no alternation in αKD cells (Figure 6D–G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D–G.

claim: Pyk2OE results in a significant increase of primary neurite number per stage 2 neuron.
source: Filopodia are thin membrane protrusion pushed by underlying actin bundles and filopodial formation is also dependent on Arp2/3 complex (Mattila and Lappalainen, 2008), we found that Pyk2OE results in a significant increase of filopodial number per stage 1 neuron as well as of primary neurite number per stage 2 neuron despite no alternation in αKD cells (Figure 6D–G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D–G.

claim: αKD cells show no alternation in filopodial number per stage 1 neuron or primary neurite number per stage 2 neuron.
source: Filopodia are thin membrane protrusion pushed by underlying actin bundles and filopodial formation is also dependent on Arp2/3 complex (Mattila and Lappalainen, 2008), we found that Pyk2OE results in a significant increase of filopodial number per stage 1 neuron as well as of primary neurite number per stage 2 neuron despite no alternation in αKD cells (Figure 6D–G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D–G.

claim: Rac1Q61L rescues both lamellipodial and filopodial defects of Pyk2OE.
source: Finally, similar to the rescue of cortical neuron migration defects of PykOE (Figure 4A), we found Rac1Q61L rescues both lamellipodial and filopodial defects of Pyk2OE (Figure 6D–G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D–G.

claim: Both αKD and Pyk2OE impact cytoskeletal dynamics, but they have subtle differences on both lamellipodia and filopodia.
source: In summary, although both αKD and Pyk2OE impact cytoskeletal dynamics, they have subtle differences on both lamellipodia and filopodia.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data comparing αKD and Pyk2OE effects on cytoskeletal structures.

claim: αKD neurons exhibit abnormal enrichment of Lifeact-labeled actin structures in stunted processes and cell bodies in the lower intermediate zone.
source: In the lower intermediate zone, αKD neurons exhibit abnormal enrichment of Lifeact-labeled actin structures in stunted processes and cell bodies, while the control neurons extend long processes with growth cones (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Pyk2OE neurons exhibit branchy morphology with multiple aberrant processes in the upper intermediate zone.
source: In the upper intermediate zone, Pyk2OE neurons exhibit branchy morphology with multiple aberrant processes; however, the control neurons have normal bipolar morphology with single leading processes and growth cones (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: A zipper-like ribbon structure assembles from combinatorial cis- and trans-interactions between like-sets of the clustered Pcdhs located in apposed plasma membranes of neighboring cells.
source: Recent studies revealed that a zipper-like ribbon structure assembles from combinatorial cis- and trans-interactions between like-sets of the clustered Pcdhs located in apposed plasma membranes of neighboring cells (Nicoludis et al., 2016; Rubinstein et al., 2015; Schreiner and Weiner, 2010; Thu et al., 2014; Wu, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Nicoludis et al., 2016; Rubinstein et al., 2015; Schreiner and Weiner, 2010; Thu et al., 2014; Wu, 2005.

claim: Protocadherin interactions could provide enormous diversity and exquisite specificity for neuronal connectivity and neurite self-avoidance required for mammalian brain development.
source: These protocadherin interactions could provide enormous diversity and exquisite specificity for neuronal connectivity and neurite self-avoidance required for mammalian brain development.
evidence: This is inferred from the known structure and function of protocadherins.

claim: Exquisite specificity is determined by strict homophilic trans-interactions of highly diversified EC2/3.
source: While exquisite specificity is determined by strict homophilic trans-interactions of highly diversified EC2/3 (Goodman et al., 2017; Molumby et al., 2016; Nicoludis et al., 2016; Rubinstein et al., 2015; Schreiner and Weiner, 2010; Thu et al., 2014; Wu, 2005); enormous diversity is mainly generated by promiscuous cis-interactions of highly conserved EC5/6 (Nicoludis et al., 2016; Rubinstein et al., 2015; Schreiner and Weiner, 2010; Thu et al., 2014; Wu, 2005).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations.

claim: Enormous diversity is mainly generated by promiscuous cis-interactions of highly conserved EC5/6.
source: While exquisite specificity is determined by strict homophilic trans-interactions of highly diversified EC2/3 (Goodman et al., 2017; Molumby et al., 2016; Nicoludis et al., 2016; Rubinstein et al., 2015; Schreiner and Weiner, 2010; Thu et al., 2014; Wu, 2005); enormous diversity is mainly generated by promiscuous cis-interactions of highly conserved EC5/6 (Nicoludis et al., 2016; Rubinstein et al., 2015; Schreiner and Weiner, 2010; Thu et al., 2014; Wu, 2005).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations.

claim: The extracellular domains of Pcdhα provide enormous diversity and exquisite specificity for cell recognition and adhesion.
source: The extracellular domains of Pcdhα provide enormous diversity and exquisite specificity for cell recognition and adhesion (Nicoludis et al., 2016; Rubinstein et al., 2015; Schreiner and Weiner, 2010; Thu et al., 2014; Wu, 2005).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations.

claim: The intracellular Pcdhα signaling pathway is largely unknown.
source: However, the intracellular Pcdhα signaling pathway is largely unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Distinct Pcdhα isoforms on the cell surface recruit WAVE complex to the cell cortex under the plasma membrane.
source: We propose a Pcdhα-based WAVE clustering model for cortical neuron migration (Figure 7). Distinct Pcdhα isoforms on the cell surface recruit WAVE complex to the cell cortex under the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is the proposed model based on the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: The WIRS motif of members of the Pcdhα family binds to a composite surface formed by Abi2 and Sra1 of the WAVE complex.
source: The WIRS motif of members of the Pcdhα family binds to a composite surface formed by Abi2 and Sra1 of the WAVE complex (Chen et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chen et al., 2014.

claim: The Pcdhα proteins may also recruit WAVE complex through the direct binding of Abi2 C-terminal SH3 domain to the four protocadherin PXXP motifs.
source: In addition, the Pcdhα proteins may also recruit WAVE complex through the direct binding of Abi2 C-terminal SH3 domain to the four protocadherin PXXP motifs, which are specific to the constant domain of the Pcdhα but not Pcdhγ family (Wu and Maniatis, 1999).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the known protein interaction domains, supported by citation to Wu and Maniatis, 1999.

claim: WAVE2 and Abi2 are required for growth cone activity during cortical neuron migration.
source: Consistently, WAVE2 and Abi2 are required for growth cone activity during cortical neuron migration (Xie et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Xie et al., 2013.

claim: N-WASP, a homolog of WAVE2, also regulates cortical neuron migration.
source: We recently found that N-WASP, a homolog of WAVE2, also regulates cortical neuron migration (Shen et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shen et al., 2018.

claim: Pyk2 has kinase-independent scaffolding activity through its FERM domain.
source: Moreover, our data suggest that Pyk2 also has kinase-independent scaffolding activity through its FERM (four-point-one, ezrin, radixin, moesin) domain, similar to the FERM domain of FAK, which binds numerous interacting partners and connects cell cortex to diverse downstream intracellular pathways (Frame et al., 2010).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data and supported by citation to Frame et al., 2010.

claim: Rac1, in conjunction with Pcdhα, activate the WAVE complex.
source: Rac1, in conjunction with Pcdhα, activate the WAVE complex (Chen et al., 2010; Lebensohn and Kirschner, 2009; Rohatgi et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chen et al., 2010; Lebensohn and Kirschner, 2009; Rohatgi et al., 1999.

claim: Two activated WAVE complexes, probably induced by protocadherin dimerization, stimulate actin-nucleating activity of Arp2/3 through the two VCAs.
source: Two activated WAVE complexes, probably induced by protocadherin dimerization, in turn stimulate actin-nucleating activity of Arp2/3 through the two VCAs (Padrick et al., 2011; Ti et al., 2011).
evidence: This is inferred from the known mechanism of WAVE complex activation, supported by citations to Padrick et al., 2011; Ti et al., 2011.

claim: The Arp2/3-mediated actin branching nucleation is central for cytoskeletal dynamics and cell motility.
source: The Arp2/3-mediated actin branching nucleation is central for cytoskeletal dynamics and cell motility (Krause and Gautreau, 2014; Lebensohn and Kirschner, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Krause and Gautreau, 2014; Lebensohn and Kirschner, 2009.

claim: Pcdhα regulates the formation and dynamics of lamellipodial and filopodial protrusions underlying cortical neuron migration through the WAVE/Pyk2/Rac1 axis.
source: Taken together, we suggest that Pcdhα regulates the formation and dynamics of lamellipodial and filopodial protrusions underlying cortical neuron migration through the WAVE/Pyk2/Rac1 axis (Figure 7).
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: αKD neurons stall in the lower intermediate zone and Pyk2OE neurons stall in the middle intermediate zone.
source: We noted that αKD neurons stall in the lower intermediate zone and Pyk2OE neurons stall in the middle intermediate zone.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: αKD phenotype is more severe than that of Pyk2OE.
source: In other words, αKD phenotype is more severe than that of Pyk2OE.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that αKD neurons stall earlier than Pyk2OE neurons.

claim: αKD neurons display stunted processes while Pyk2OE neurons have branchy morphology.
source: In addition, αKD neurons display stunted processes while Pyk2OE neurons have branchy morphology.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: In addition to disinhibition of Pyk2 and consequently inhibition of Rac1, αKD also impairs the membrane recruiting of the WAVE complex directly.
source: Consistently, the WAVE clustering model suggests that, in addition to disinhibition of Pyk2 and consequently inhibition of Rac1, αKD also impairs the membrane recruiting of the WAVE complex directly (Figure 7).
evidence: This is inferred from the WAVE clustering model and the experimental data.

claim: αc2 endows serotonergic neurons with a single cell-type identity and specifically mediates the axonal tiling and assembly of serotonergic neural circuitries.
source: However, a recent study revealed an intriguing role of αc2 in serotonergic axonal local tiling and global assembly (Chen et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chen et al., 2017.

claim: The unique sequences of the αc2 variable cytoplasmic domain may restrict its role to axonal tiling of serotonergic neurons but not cortical neuron migration.
source: Given the known role of variable cytoplasmic domain of clustered Pcdh proteins in their cytoplasmic association (Shonubi et al., 2015), the unique sequences of the αc2 variable cytoplasmic domain may restrict its role to axonal tiling of serotonergic neurons but not cortical neuron migration.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the known role of variable cytoplasmic domains, supported by citation to Shonubi et al., 2015.

claim: Diverse roles of the clustered Pcdh genes in axonal targeting, dendritic tiling and self-avoidance, spine morphogenesis, synaptogenesis and connectivity have been reported.
source: Diverse roles of the clustered Pcdh genes in axonal targeting, dendritic tiling and self-avoidance, spine morphogenesis, synaptogenesis and connectivity have been reported (Garrett et al., 2012; Katori et al., 2009; Lefebvre et al., 2012; Molumby et al., 2016; Rubinstein et al., 2015; Suo et al., 2012; Thu et al., 2014; Zipursky and Sanes, 2010).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations.

claim: Pcdhα functions in axonal projection of olfactory sensory and serotonergic neurons.
source: In particular, genetic studies demonstrated that Pcdhα functions in axonal projection of olfactory sensory and serotonergic neurons (Chen et al., 2017; Hasegawa et al., 2008; Katori et al., 2009; Mountoufaris et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chen et al., 2017; Hasegawa et al., 2008; Katori et al., 2009; Mountoufaris et al., 2017.

claim: Celsr3 is central for interneuron tangential migration and Globus Pallidus axonal connectivity in the mouse forebrain.
source: In addition, another WIRS-containing protocadherin, Celsr3, is also central for interneuron tangential migration and Globus Pallidus axonal connectivity in the mouse forebrain (Jia et al., 2014; Ying et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jia et al., 2014; Ying et al., 2009.

claim: The WIRS domain point mutation rescues the Pcdhα dominant-negative effects on dendrite outgrowth and branching of primary cultured cortical neurons.
source: Sholl analysis demonstrated that the WIRS domain point mutation rescues the Pcdhα dominant-negative effects on dendrite outgrowth and branching of primary cultured cortical neurons, suggesting that the Pcdhα/WAVE/Pyk2/Rac1 signaling axis indeed functions in dendrite morphogenesis (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by Sholl analysis data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The Pcdhα/WAVE/Pyk2/Rac1 signaling axis functions in dendrite morphogenesis.
source: Sholl analysis demonstrated that the WIRS domain point mutation rescues the Pcdhα dominant-negative effects on dendrite outgrowth and branching of primary cultured cortical neurons, suggesting that the Pcdhα/WAVE/Pyk2/Rac1 signaling axis indeed functions in dendrite morphogenesis (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the Sholl analysis data.

claim: The regulation of neuronal migration and neurite development by the Pcdhα/WAVE/Pyk2/Rac1 axis through actin cytoskeletal dynamics may be a general mechanism for diverse roles of protocadherins in brain development and function.
source: Thus, the regulation of neuronal migration and neurite development by the Pcdhα/WAVE/Pyk2/Rac1 axis through actin cytoskeletal dynamics may be a general mechanism for diverse roles of protocadherins in brain development and function.
evidence: This is a speculation about the broader implications of the findings.
